html:
The Third Council of Constantinople, held in 680 and 681, is counted as the sixth ecumenical council by the Orthodox and Catholic churches. Emperor Constantine IV called it to end a quarrel that had split the church for fifty years.

The quarrel was over monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had only one will. Emperor Heraclius had backed it as a compromise to win over Christians in Egypt and Syria who rejected the Council of Chalcedon. By 680 those lands had been lost in the Arab conquests, and the compromise no longer served any purpose.

The council declared that Christ has two wills, divine and human, working in harmony. It condemned the leading backers of the one-will teaching, among them Pope Honorius I, who had died decades earlier. Later Catholic debates on papal infallibility kept returning to this case of a pope condemned as a heretic.
sum: The Third Council of Constantinople, held in 680 and 681, is counted as the sixth ecumenical council by the Orthodox and Catholic churches. Emperor Constantine IV called it to end a quarrel that had split the church for fifty years.
